title: Drill a shallow hole at a marked point on a wood block using both arms
instruction: Use the right arm to hold the drill and the left arm to pull its red trigger. Drill a vertical 6 mm hole, 10 to 13 mm deep, at the centre of the red target on the secured wood block. Withdraw the bit and release the trigger when finished.
context: Drilling a marked hole for a shelf, bracket or other home project is a familiar use of a cordless drill. The robot must keep the bit centred and upright while coordinating the trigger and downward feed against resistance, then withdraw the bit and stop the tool.
setup: World coordinates are metres: X forward from the arm bases, Y left, Z up. Two 6-DoF YAM arms with parallel grippers have bases at (0, +0.305, 0.750) and (0, -0.305, 0.750). Both start at joint angles [0, 1, 1, -0.6, 0, 0] radians with 94 mm open jaws. A fixed wood-appearance table is 1.10 x 1.30 x 0.06 m, centred at (0.36, 0, 0.7175); its top is Z=0.7475. A secured dry clear-pine block, 180 x 140 x 30 mm, is centred at (0.260, -0.080, 0.7625), with top Z=0.7775; grain runs along world X, its 180 mm dimension. The wood starts unbored. A 20 mm diameter red target is centred on its top; its 0.4 mm visual overlay has no collider. The orange/black plastic-housing and metal-chuck drill body is approximately 184.36 x 186.84 x 57.19 mm and 0.5 kg. It starts on its side with the original body bounding-box centre at XY (0.250, -0.300), yaw 90 degrees, chuck pointing along world -Y. A 6 mm steel twist-bit approximation, 35 mm long and 6 mm diameter, extends the chuck: its model-frame end is (-0.127, -0.0695, 0). The assembled drill/bit extent is about 219.18 x 186.84 x 57.19 mm. A red polymer trigger proxy, 14 x 20 x 40 mm and 15 g, is attached at drill model coordinate (-0.017, -0.017, 0), with 5 mm travel in model +X, 150 N/m return stiffness and 2 N s/m damping. The workpiece securing fixture is approximated by a fixed body. The calibrated station also includes a floor, fixed overhead RGB camera and collision stand/housing, lights, and one RGB camera on each wrist; README documents these shared fixtures and pinned sources. All starts use seed 0, zero jitter, and a 0.5-second settling phase before the trial.
scoring: Full score requires a 6 mm bore with entry centre within 3 mm of the target centre, bore axis within 12 degrees of downward vertical, and depth 10 to 13 mm. At least 10 mm of cutting progress must occur while the right gripper holds the handle with both pads and the left fingertips depress the attached trigger at least 3 mm. Finish holding the drill with its bit at least 15 mm above the wood and the trigger released (at most 1 mm stroke) for 0.5 seconds. The physical trial checks the hole centre and depth with a ruler and depth probe, angle with a protractor, and the two-arm operation and release in video. Simulation grasp/contact detectors require each right pad and the left trigger contact above 0.05 N; right TCP within 55 mm of the handle, jaw gap below 75 mm. These low contact thresholds detect contact, not drilling force. Cutting itself needs at least 8 N of material reaction and a rotating spindle. Award 0 for no grasp, no steps, or a hole at least 2 mm deep outside the location/angle limits, or any depth over 13 mm. Otherwise award 0.25 for holding the drill; 0.50 for at least 2 mm of qualifying on-target cutting; 0.75 for a complete qualifying hole before the final withdrawal/release hold; 1.0 after that hold.
run_limit: 2,400 control steps at 20 Hz: 120 seconds of simulation time. Full success ends the run early.
reset_notes: Use a fresh dry pine coupon with the specified dimensions, target and grain orientation for each physical trial; secure it in the same bench-clamp positions. Simulator reset clears the bore, material history and spindle, restores the drill/trigger and both open-jaw ready poses, and settles for 0.5 s. Seed 0, zero jitter.
fidelity: PhysX 240 Hz, YAM control 20 Hz. A compliant single-bore model applies feed resistance and reaction torque to the drill; trigger travel drives spindle speed. Depth follows measured bit motion under load, with persistent visible bore geometry. Wood is fixed. The trigger proxy, inertias and softwood force law are approximate and not bench calibrated. No chips, fracture or heat. The bit/wood pair uses this material law; other collisions remain rigid.
